metadata.description: Learn ten breast changes worth checking, who may be at greater risk, how breast-clinic tests work and what can happen after a diagnosis.
metadata.title: 10 Breast Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

landing.title: 10 Breast Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
landing.intro: Some are surprisingly easy to miss — and several have nothing to do with finding a lump.

icon.alt: Illustration of a woman raising her arm with a breast area highlighted

disclaimer: General information only. This article is not a diagnosis, medical assessment or substitute for advice from a qualified healthcare professional. Breast cancer can affect people of any sex. Have a new or unusual breast, chest or armpit change assessed rather than relying on an online description.

sections.title: 10 Breast Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
sections.intro: Most breast changes are not cancer, and breast cancer does not always begin with a noticeable lump. Knowing what is normal for you makes a new, persistent or unusual change easier to recognise and explain.

points.title: A new lump or firm area in the breast or chest
paragraphs: You may notice a lump, thickened area or firmness that feels different from the surrounding tissue or from the same area on the other side.
Cysts, hormonal changes and other benign conditions commonly cause lumps. A new lump should still be assessed rather than diagnosed by touch alone.

points.title: Swelling or a lump in the armpit
paragraphs: A new swelling or firm node may appear beneath the arm, sometimes before a change in the breast is obvious.
Infections, inflammation and recent vaccinations can also enlarge lymph nodes. A lump that persists, grows or has no clear explanation deserves medical review.

points.title: A change in breast size, shape or outline
paragraphs: One breast may begin to look larger, lower, swollen or shaped differently from its usual appearance.
Natural asymmetry is common and bodies change over time. The concern is a new or unexplained difference, particularly when it appears with another skin or nipple change.

points.title: Skin dimpling or puckering
paragraphs: The skin may pull inward, form small dents or take on a pitted texture sometimes compared with orange peel.
Scarring, previous surgery and inflammation can alter breast skin too. New dimpling or tethering should be examined promptly.

points.title: Redness, swelling or warmth that does not settle
paragraphs: Part or all of a breast may look red or darker than the surrounding skin, feel swollen or unusually warm, or seem heavier.
Infection is a common cause, especially during breastfeeding, but persistent or worsening inflammation needs assessment. Rare inflammatory breast cancer may not form a distinct lump.

points.title: A nipple that turns inward or changes position
paragraphs: A nipple may begin pulling inward, point in a new direction or look noticeably different from its usual position.
Some nipples have always been inverted and harmless changes can occur. A new retraction or distortion is the pattern that should be discussed with a clinician.

points.title: Unexpected nipple discharge
paragraphs: Fluid may appear without squeezing, particularly from one nipple. It may be clear, cloudy or blood-stained.
Discharge has many possible causes, including medicines and benign duct changes. New spontaneous discharge, especially when blood-stained, needs assessment.

points.title: A rash, crusting or sore around the nipple
paragraphs: The nipple or surrounding darker skin may become scaly, crusted, persistently irritated or develop a sore that does not heal.
Eczema and contact irritation are much more common explanations. A one-sided change that persists or does not respond as expected should be checked.

points.title: Persistent breast or armpit pain
paragraphs: Pain may remain in one specific area rather than following a familiar monthly or activity-related pattern.
Breast pain by itself is not usually caused by cancer. Persistent, unexplained or worsening pain still deserves assessment, especially with a lump or visible change.

points.title: A change that simply looks or feels unusual for you
paragraphs: The first sign may be difficult to name: a different texture, fullness, pulling sensation or visual change that was not present before.
You do not need to match a perfect checklist before seeking advice. A continuing change from your normal is enough reason to arrange a professional examination.

next.title: But Who Is Most At Risk?
next.copy: Symptoms are only part of the picture. Age, family history, breast density and several less obvious factors can affect a person's underlying risk.

sections.title: Breast Cancer Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: Risk factors change probability, not certainty. Many people diagnosed with breast cancer have no strong family history, while most people with one or more risk factors never develop it.

points.title: Age
paragraphs: Breast-cancer risk increases with age. Most diagnoses occur in older adults, although the disease can affect younger people too.

points.title: Sex and lifetime hormone exposure
paragraphs: Breast cancer is far more common in women, partly because of breast tissue and lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone. Men and people of other genders can still develop it.

points.title: A previous breast-cancer diagnosis
paragraphs: Someone previously treated for breast cancer can have a higher chance of recurrence or a new cancer in either breast. Follow-up advice depends on the original diagnosis and treatment.

points.title: Certain previous breast-cell changes
paragraphs: Some biopsy findings, such as atypical hyperplasia or lobular carcinoma in situ, can be markers of increased future risk. They are not the same as invasive breast cancer and need individual interpretation.

points.title: A close family history
paragraphs: Risk may be higher when close relatives have had breast cancer, particularly when several relatives were affected, diagnoses occurred unusually young or cancer affected both breasts.
Family patterns involving ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer can also matter when they suggest an inherited genetic change; one isolated diagnosis does not prove an inherited syndrome.

points.title: Inherited genetic changes
paragraphs: Harmful changes in genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 can substantially increase risk. These inherited changes account for only a minority of breast cancers and genetic testing should be guided by appropriate counselling.

points.title: Dense breast tissue
paragraphs: Dense breasts contain more fibrous and glandular tissue relative to fat. Density can both raise risk and make mammograms harder to interpret, but it cannot be reliably judged by touch or appearance.

points.title: Previous radiotherapy to the chest
paragraphs: Radiotherapy involving the chest at a young age, for example for some lymphomas, can increase later breast-cancer risk. The level of surveillance depends on age, dose and treatment history.

points.title: Alcohol, weight and physical activity
paragraphs: Alcohol is an established breast-cancer risk factor. Higher body weight after menopause and lower physical activity are also associated with increased risk, although no lifestyle can guarantee prevention.

points.title: Hormone therapy and reproductive history
paragraphs: Some forms and durations of menopausal hormone therapy can increase risk, while reproductive and menstrual history can influence lifetime hormone exposure.
These factors need context. Risk information does not diagnose cancer and should not be used to stop prescribed medicine without discussing benefits and alternatives with a clinician.

sections.title: What Actually Happens During A Breast Cancer Check?
sections.intro: No single test answers every question. A breast clinic or specialist service usually combines examination, imaging and tissue testing when needed, and not everyone requires every test.

points.title: Symptoms and medical or family history
paragraphs: A clinician asks what changed, when it began and whether it is progressing. Previous breast problems, medicines, pregnancy or breastfeeding, menstrual or menopausal history and relevant cancers in the family can add context.

points.title: A breast, chest and lymph-node examination
paragraphs: The clinician may examine both breasts or the chest, the nipples and nearby lymph-node areas such as the armpits. They assess the location, mobility and texture of any lump as well as visible changes.

points.title: Diagnostic mammography
paragraphs: A mammogram uses low-dose X-rays to look for masses, calcifications and other changes. Diagnostic views can focus on the area of concern and differ from routine screening images.

points.title: Breast ultrasound
paragraphs: Ultrasound uses sound waves to examine a specific area and can help distinguish a fluid-filled cyst from a solid mass. It is often used alongside mammography rather than as a universal replacement.

callouts.question: Does finding a lump mean cancer?
callouts.answer: No. Many breast lumps are cysts, fibroadenomas or other benign changes, but examination and imaging are needed to identify the cause.

callouts.question: Can one normal test rule out every breast cancer?
callouts.answer: Not always. Clinicians compare symptoms, examination and imaging and may arrange another test when the findings do not explain the change.

callouts.question: Does everyone with a breast change need a biopsy?
callouts.answer: No. A biopsy is used when imaging or examination leaves an area that needs tissue diagnosis.

points.title: Needle biopsy where needed
paragraphs: A core-needle biopsy commonly removes small tissue samples from a suspicious area, usually using local anaesthetic and imaging guidance. The sample is examined under a microscope to determine whether abnormal or cancer cells are present.

points.title: The pathology and biomarker report
paragraphs: If cancer is found, pathology identifies the type and grade. Testing commonly assesses oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 status because these biomarkers help guide treatment choices.

sections.title: What Happens If Doctors Find Something?
sections.intro: An abnormal scan or biopsy result is not one single diagnosis. The team combines pathology, imaging and personal circumstances before explaining what has been found and which options are appropriate.

points.title: The result may be benign
paragraphs: Tests can identify a cyst, fibroadenoma, inflammation, fat necrosis or another non-cancerous condition. Some need no treatment, while others are monitored or managed because of symptoms.

points.title: Atypical cells or DCIS are found
paragraphs: Atypical cell changes can indicate increased risk or need further removal. Ductal carcinoma in situ, or DCIS, means abnormal cells are contained within breast ducts and have not invaded surrounding breast tissue.
These findings are not interchangeable. Their extent and pathology determine whether surgery, monitoring or another treatment is discussed.

points.title: Invasive breast cancer is confirmed
paragraphs: Invasive cancer has grown beyond the ducts or lobules where it began. The specialist team identifies the subtype and assesses what further information is needed before recommending treatment.

points.title: What type and grade mean
paragraphs: Type describes where the cancer began and its microscopic pattern. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look and gives an indication of how quickly they may grow and spread.

points.title: Why ER, PR and HER2 results matter
paragraphs: Hormone-receptor and HER2 results reveal biological features that can be targeted by endocrine or HER2-directed medicines. A cancer lacking all three markers is described as triple-negative and follows a different treatment pathway.

points.title: How stage and lymph nodes are assessed
paragraphs: Stage considers tumour size and location, nearby lymph nodes, spread elsewhere, grade and biomarkers. Examination, breast imaging, biopsy and sometimes additional scans or sentinel lymph-node biopsy contribute to this assessment.

points.title: The main treatment routes doctors may discuss
paragraphs: Depending on the diagnosis, options may include breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy. Treatment can be given before or after surgery, and many people receive more than one type.
The plan reflects stage, tumour biology, general health and personal preferences. One person's treatment is not a reliable guide to what another person will need.

sections.title: Breast Cancer Outlook: What Really Matters
sections.intro: Outlook varies widely between breast-cancer types and individuals. Doctors combine several clinical and biological factors rather than relying on one symptom, scan or statistic.

points.title: Whether the cancer is localised
paragraphs: Cancer confined to the breast generally has more treatment options intended to cure than disease that has spread to distant organs. Its exact position and extent still influence surgery and radiotherapy choices.

points.title: Tumour size and nearby structures
paragraphs: Size contributes to stage, but it is not interpreted alone. Doctors also consider whether the tumour involves skin, the chest wall or more than one part of the breast.

points.title: Lymph-node involvement
paragraphs: Cancer in nearby lymph nodes changes the stage and can affect recommendations for surgery, radiotherapy and medicines. The number and location of involved nodes also matter.

points.title: Whether it has spread elsewhere
paragraphs: Distant or metastatic breast cancer is treated differently from cancer confined to the breast and nearby nodes. Treatment often aims to control disease, reduce symptoms and maintain quality of life for as long as possible.

points.title: Grade and growth rate
paragraphs: Higher-grade cells generally look more abnormal and may grow more quickly. Grade adds important context but does not replace stage or biomarker information.

points.title: Hormone receptors, HER2 and other biomarkers
paragraphs: Biomarkers describe possible treatment targets and help explain why two cancers at the same anatomical stage may be treated differently. Some tumours are also assessed with multigene tests when clinically appropriate.

points.title: Response to treatment
paragraphs: When medicine is given before surgery, the response can provide useful biological information. During and after treatment, examinations, scans and other results help the team judge what should happen next.

points.title: Age, general health and treatment tolerance
paragraphs: Overall health, other medical conditions and personal priorities affect which treatments are suitable. Age alone does not determine whether someone can benefit from treatment.

points.title: Why statistics cannot predict one person's future
paragraphs: Survival figures describe large groups diagnosed in the past. They cannot fully account for one person's tumour biology, health, response or access to newer treatment.
Finding cancer earlier can widen the available options, but no statistic or early sign guarantees an individual outcome.

conclusion.copy: Breast cancers can behave very differently from one person to another. A lump, mammogram or even one pathology result cannot establish an individual's outlook on its own. Doctors combine stage, grade, biomarkers, general health and response to treatment before discussing what happens next.
